patrimoine.apropos.m1: Profiles to be enriched, together. The profiles are taken from the INP’s public data (for the time being: historical and architectural heritage only). The idea is that every citizen should help to edit and enrich them.
patrimoine.apropos.m2: Contribute. Access is free and requires no login details. By clicking on a site, anyone can fill in a supplementary entry — photos if available, history, captions, additional information. To contribute, you only need to provide your surname, first name and email address.
patrimoine.apropos.m3: Moderation before publication. Once submitted, the entry goes through moderation to prevent any misuse or the dissemination of inappropriate material. No contribution is published automatically. Final approval or rejection would be the responsibility of a panel of experts. We would like to see members of the INP on this panel, and the invitation is open to them — but this is, as yet, merely a wish. The reasons for acceptance or rejection are visible.
patrimoine.apropos.m4: Once published, anyone can comment on or add to it; the panel will approve (or reject) any additions to the final entry.
patrimoine.apropos.m5: Photos. If you publish a photo you have taken, you agree to transfer the rights to publish it — but you remain the owner, are credited and cited each time it is used, without compensation.
patrimoine.apropos.m6: Governance. Identifiable and recognised moderators have limited access to contributions and are responsible for publishing them online. The panel of experts would have its own access; the administration oversees the whole process. The precise rules are yet to be defined.
patrimoine.apropos.m7: Always free. No financial contribution is requested, nor will any be requested. Any attempt to use this platform to raise money does not originate from us. The content of the fact sheets is downloadable in PDF and HTML at any time, and is kept up to date. A ‘Follow us’ section will allow users to receive notifications. The content is freely accessible: if others wish to use it to raise funds for conservation, they are free to do so — this will be a separate initiative, unrelated to ours.

patrimoine.intro.inp: ⚠️ The partnership with the INP is currently a hope, not a done deal: the invitation remains open to them. To date, no agreement has been reached. The fact sheets use their public data as a starting point. Watch this space.
patrimoine.intro.n1: A private, solo and free initiative to help identify Tunisia’s heritage — be it architectural, human, social, cultural or historical. There is no company or organisation behind it: just a great deal of time spent, alone, coding it and keeping it running.
patrimoine.intro.n2: At present, the only database available is that of the National Heritage Institute (INP). It is missing a great deal: royalty-free photos, recent and comprehensive information on the actual condition of the sites, and details of whether or not there is an urgent need for conservation.
patrimoine.intro.n3: Here, we do not collect money: this is neither our raison d’être nor an objective. However, information that has been gathered, verified and consolidated into a single document could serve as a starting point for others to initiate conservation efforts.
patrimoine.intro.n4: This list serves to open our eyes to a heritage that we live alongside without always being aware of it, to look after it, and to remain vigilant against abuses.
patrimoine.intro.n5: The heritage section is part of a broader app — available on the App Store, coming soon to the Play Store, and already available as a web version (PWA). This app is free for 15 days, after which a fee applies; however, access to the heritage section remains open, in several languages, beyond the two-week period — and for life. The paid section never encroaches on the heritage section: the two are independent of one another.
patrimoine.lead: The database of listed heritage sites — their condition, classification and location. Open to all. Find a site, keep an eye on it, report what you see.
patrimoine.legal.l1: Information provided for guidance only. The information presented — including contributions from members of the public — is provided for guidance only, without any guarantee of accuracy, completeness or timeliness.
patrimoine.legal.l2: User-generated content. The texts, photos and comments published are the sole responsibility of their authors. Despite moderation, errors or inappropriate content may remain: any content may be reported and removed upon request.
patrimoine.legal.l3: Photo rights. By submitting a photograph, the contributor warrants that they hold the rights to it (or that it is royalty-free) and authorises its publication. They remain the owner and are credited. In the event of a claim by a rights holder, the photograph will be removed upon request.
patrimoine.legal.l4: Personal data. The surname, first name and email address provided for the purpose of contributing are used solely to manage and moderate contributions and, where necessary, to contact you. They are neither resold nor transferred. You may request to view, correct or delete your data via the contact details below.
patrimoine.legal.l5: Non-profit status. This initiative does not raise any funds. Any requests for financial contributions made in its name are unrelated to it.
patrimoine.legal.l6: Trademarks and third parties. The names and trademarks mentioned (including the INP) belong to their respective owners; their mention does not imply any connection or endorsement.
patrimoine.legal.l7: Limitation of liability. The service is provided ‘as is’. To the extent permitted by law, the initiative accepts no liability for any damage resulting from its use or unavailability.
patrimoine.legal.l8: Reporting & contact. To report abuse, request removal or exercise your rights: {contact}.

abbir maius.a: The scattered remains of the ancient Roman city in the El Fahs region, known primarily for its inscriptions.
abbir maius.c: A site in a state of advanced ruin, best suited to enthusiasts of epigraphy and archaeology; a local guide is recommended.
abbir maius.d: Ancient Roman city in the El Fahs region (Zaghouan), known for its inscriptions and ruins.

abthugni (henchir es-souar).a: The remains of the forum, a temple and municipal features of the Roman city, scattered across the countryside in the south of the governorate.
abthugni (henchir es-souar).c: A modest site with few facilities for enthusiasts; a vehicle is essential and local guidance is recommended.
abthugni (henchir es-souar).d: Roman city in the south of the Zaghouan governorate, featuring a forum, a temple and municipal ruins.

acholla (botria).a: A Punic and later Roman city on the Sahel coast, known for some of the oldest mosaics in Tunisia (now in the Bardo), a forum, two thermal baths and houses.
acholla (botria).c: The finest mosaics are in the Bardo Museum; whilst there, do arrange for a guide to help you interpret the ruins.
acholla (botria).d: A Punic and later Roman city on the Sahel coast, near Botria. It features some of the oldest Roman-African mosaics in Tunisia (at the Bardo), a forum, two thermal baths and houses.

agbia (ain hedja).a: The late Byzantine fortified post stands on a hill overlooking the ancient Roman road, alongside the scattered remains of the Numidian-Roman city.
agbia (ain hedja).c: A short stop near Dougga; a brief climb, but make sure you wear sturdy shoes.
agbia (ain hedja).d: A Numidian and later Roman city (Municipium Agbiensium) near Dougga. A late Byzantine fort on a hill overlooking the ancient Roman road.

aiguilles de tabarka.a: The sandstone spires rising from the seashore, an iconic rock formation on the Tabarka coast.
aiguilles de tabarka.c: A great spot for photos at sunset; well worth combining with a visit to the Genoese fort and the coral coast.
aiguilles de tabarka.d: Remarkable rock formation on the Tabarka coast: sandstone spires rising from the seashore.

ain draham (kroumirie).a: The cork oak forests; houses with red-tiled roofs; footpaths and viewpoints overlooking the wooded mountains.
ain draham (kroumirie).c: The country’s rainiest region: lush and green in spring, sometimes snow-covered in winter – do bring a jacket.
ain draham (kroumirie).d: A mountain resort in the heart of the Kroumirie cork oak forests, one of Tunisia’s rainiest regions. Coordinates centred on the town.

ain kriz.a: Natural spring north of Tozeur, in the El Oudiane oasis group (Jerid).
ain kriz.c: A refreshing stop in the palm grove; please respect the spring’s facilities.
ain kriz.d: Natural spring north of Tozeur, in the El Oudiane oasis group (Jerid).

ajim (djerba).a: A port in the west of Djerba, the main ferry link to the mainland and a former sponge-fishing port.
ajim (djerba).c: The ferry connects Djerba to the mainland: allow for waiting times during peak hours.
ajim (djerba).d: A coastal town in the west of Djerba, the main ferry link to the mainland and a former sponge-fishing port.

akouda.a: A town north-west of Sousse, characterised by the minaret of its Great Mosque.
akouda.c: A brief stop; of interest mainly for the minaret and the old town centre.
akouda.d: A town north-west of Sousse, characterised by the minaret of its Great Mosque.

al-mansuriya (sabra).a: Heavily levelled remains of a Fatimid and later Zirid palatial city, now largely lost; of mainly archaeological interest.
al-mansuriya (sabra).c: Site poorly developed and difficult to interpret: best suited to archaeology enthusiasts, ideally accompanied by a guide.
al-mansuriya (sabra).d: Former Fatimid and later Zirid palatial city near Kairouan, now largely lost. Approximate coordinates of the site.

althiburos (el medeina).a: The forum, temples, theatre, arch and mosaic-decorated houses of one of the oldest known Numidian settlements.
althiburos (el medeina).c: Near Dahmani; make sure you bring water and allow about 1½ hours to explore this extensive and largely undeveloped site.
althiburos (el medeina).d: A Numidian and later Roman city in the delegation of Dahmani (Le Kef), one of the oldest known Numidian settlements. Forum, temples, theatre, arch and mosaic-decorated houses.

amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).a: The superimposed arcades of the façade; the arena and the underground passages through which animals and gladiators passed; the tiers of seating that you can climb.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).c: Climb to the upper levels for the view; combine your visit with the El Jem Museum and its mosaics.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).d: The grand Roman amphitheatre of ancient Thysdrus, dating from the 3rd century, is one of the best-preserved in the world. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

amphitheatre de bararus.a: Remains of a Roman amphitheatre at the Bararus (Rougga) site, south-east of El Jem.
amphitheatre de bararus.c: Well worth visiting alongside the rest of the Rougga site, for lovers of antiquity.
amphitheatre de bararus.d: Roman amphitheatre at the ancient site of Bararus (Rougga), south-east of El Jem.

amphitheatre de carthage.a: The levelled arena and the commemorative cross marking the martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicity; the remains of the stands.
amphitheatre de carthage.c: A modest site, best included as part of a wider tour of the ruins of Carthage.
amphitheatre de carthage.d: The amphitheatre of Roman Carthage, largely levelled, is traditionally associated with the martyrdom of Saints Perpetua and Felicity.
amphitheatre de carthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

amphitheatre de tebourba.a: The levelled remains of the Roman amphitheatre of ancient Thuburbo Minus, set within the modern town; a modest site.
amphitheatre de tebourba.c: A quick visit to include as part of a stroll through Tebourba.
amphitheatre de tebourba.d: Remains of the Roman amphitheatre of ancient Thuburbo Minus, in Tebourba.

apisa maius.a: The remains of a city in Proconsular Africa and a former episcopal see (Tarf ech Chenah).
apisa maius.c: Near Bou Arada; an unassuming rural site, particularly for archaeology enthusiasts.
apisa maius.d: Ancient city of Proconsular Africa and episcopal see (Tarf ech Chenah), near Bou Arada.

aqueduc de zaghouan a carthage.a: The long rows of Roman arches still standing in the plain, remnants of the more than 130 km of aqueduct that carried water from Zaghouan to Carthage.
aqueduc de zaghouan a carthage.c: The arches are clearly visible from the Tunis–Zaghouan road, particularly towards Mohammedia/Oudhna; beautiful low-angle light at the end of the day.
aqueduc de zaghouan a carthage.d: A Roman aqueduct stretching over 130 km, carrying water from the springs of Zaghouan to Carthage; long rows of arches are still visible. Coordinates of a section.

arc de gordien iii (musti / el krib).a: A monumental arch dating from 239, marking an eastern entrance to ancient Musti.
arc de gordien iii (musti / el krib).c: Highlight of the Musti site; a quick visit whilst walking around the site.
arc de gordien iii (musti / el krib).d: Monumental arch of ancient Musti (El Krib), dated 239 according to an inscription, marking one of the eastern entrances to the city (a ceremonial gate rather than a triumphal arch). Coordinates within the site are approximate.

arc romain de zaghouan.a: The Roman arch (monumental gate) still standing in the town, at the foot of the path leading up to the Temple of the Waters.
arc romain de zaghouan.c: A stop on the way to the Temple of the Waters; a short break.
arc romain de zaghouan.d: A triumphal arch / Roman gate still standing in the town of Zaghouan, at the foot of the Temple of the Waters.

archipel de la galite.a: The volcanic archipelago off the northern coast of Tunisia, the country’s northernmost point, a former monk seal habitat, now a protected area.
archipel de la galite.c: Access is by boat only and weather permitting: plan an organised excursion during the summer months from Bizerte or Tabarka.
archipel de la galite.d: Volcanic archipelago off the northern coast of Tunisia, the country’s northernmost point. Protected area, former monk seal habitat.

assuras (henchir zanfour).a: The temples, theatre and Augustan mausoleums of this Roman city, which later became a bishop’s seat.
assuras (henchir zanfour).c: A rural site between Siliana and Le Sers, with few signposts: a guide or precise coordinates will help you find it.
assuras (henchir zanfour).d: A Roman town in Proconsular Africa, between Siliana and the Sers. Temples, a theatre and Augustan mausoleums; an episcopal see from the mid-3rd century.

atelier de potier de sidi bouzid.a: Ancient potter’s workshop listed as a historic monument, near the town of Sidi Bouzid.
atelier de potier de sidi bouzid.c: Specialised site: best visited with a guide to fully appreciate its significance.
atelier de potier de sidi bouzid.d: Ancient potter’s workshop listed as a historic monument, near the town of Sidi Bouzid.

avitta bibba (henchir bou ftis).a: The scattered remains of the Roman city, including the ruins of an amphitheatre, in the countryside near Bou Arada; a modest site with little infrastructure.
avitta bibba (henchir bou ftis).c: For archaeology enthusiasts only; you’ll need a car and should ask locals for directions to find it.
avitta bibba (henchir bou ftis).d: Roman city of Africa Proconsularis near Bou Arada, north of Siliana (Henchir Bou Ftis). Former episcopal see; remains of an amphitheatre.

bab alioua.a: The south-eastern gate of the medina, the historic starting point for the routes to the Sahel and the south of the country, now situated in a very busy transport hub.
bab alioua.c: A busy crossroads: simply a landmark, with no interior to visit.
bab alioua.d: The south-eastern gate of the medina of Tunis, the historic starting point for the routes to the Sahel and the south.

bab bnet.a: Nearby: the Collège Sadiki (1875), the cradle of Tunisian modernity, which overlooks the medina with its minaret and domes.
bab bnet.c: Well worth a look as you make your way from Kasbah Square to the medina.
bab bnet.d: A neighbourhood in the western part of the medina, near the administrative kasbah, which takes its name from one of the oldest gates (built around 1228–1249), which no longer exists. The name now refers to the neighbourhood itself.

bab diwan (sfax).a: The main gate of the medina, on the southern side of the ramparts; for a long time one of the city’s only two entrances.
bab diwan (sfax).c: An ideal starting point for a walking tour of the medina.
bab diwan (sfax).d: The main gate of the Sfax medina, on the southern face of the ramparts. Until the 20th century, the medina had only two entrances: Bab Diwan and Bab Jebli.

bab el allouj.a: The former gate on the north-western side of the walls, near the Kasbah, a remnant of the medina’s gate system.
bab el allouj.c: A brief stop to be combined with visits to the other gates in the Kasbah area.
bab el allouj.d: Former gate in the walls of the Tunis medina, on the north-western side, near the kasbah.

bab el assel.a: The El Borj (Sidi Yahia) Mosque; the picturesque ‘Rue du Miel’.
bab el assel.c: In the heart of the working-class northern part of the medina, on the way to Bab Souika and Halfaouine.
bab el assel.d: A neighbourhood in the northern part of the medina (Bab Souika area), centred around an ancient gate. Its name is thought to derive from the Bani Assal family who lived there – or from the word for honey (‘assel’): the nearby ‘Rue du Miel’ (Honey Street) bears witness to this. The gate is also known as Bab Sidi Yahya, named after the neighbouring El Borj (Sidi Yahia) Mosque.

bab el bhar (porte de france).a: The monumental arch marking the entrance to the medina of Tunis, the dividing line between the Arab quarter and the European quarter.
bab el bhar (porte de france).c: A central landmark and the ideal starting point for a tour of the medina from Avenue Bourguiba.
bab el bhar (porte de france).d: A historic gate marking the boundary between the medina of Tunis and the European quarter, nicknamed the ‘Gate of France’. The arch has stood alone since the demolition of the city walls.

bab el fellah.a: The neighbourhood leads to the mosque and mausoleum of Sidi Béchir Ziri, founder of a Rahmania zaouïa.
bab el fellah.c: A quick stop on the southern edge of the medina.
bab el fellah.d: A neighbourhood to the south of the medina, named after a gate that disappeared around 1890 and which opened onto the southern suburbs (cemeteries and zaouias). The gate no longer exists; the name remains for the neighbourhood.

bab el jazira.a: On El Jazira Square: the Bab Jazira Mosque (known as the ‘funeral mosque’), and just a stone’s throw away, the Sidi El Béchir Mosque.
bab el jazira.c: A lively, working-class neighbourhood; well worth a quick visit to complement a stroll through the lower medina.
bab el jazira.d: The southern quarter of the medina, which takes its name from a former gate – the oldest on the southern rampart, opening towards the south and Kairouan – which disappeared during the Protectorate (its role was taken over by Bab Alioua). Today, the name refers to this lively, working-class neighbourhood.

bab el khadra.a: The gate, rebuilt in the 19th century to the north of the medina, whose name evokes the ancient gardens beyond the ramparts.
bab el khadra.c: A quick stop on the northern edge of the medina.
bab el khadra.d: A gate to the north of the medina of Tunis, rebuilt in the 19th century; its name evokes the gardens beyond the ramparts.

bab jebli (sfax).a: The second historic gate of the medina, on the northern side of the ramparts, leading to the food souks.
bab jebli (sfax).c: The more popular northern side: a good gateway to the hustle and bustle of daily life.
bab jebli (sfax).d: The second historic gate of the Sfax medina, on the northern side of the ramparts.

bab jedid.a: The rare medieval Hafsid gate still standing in the south of the medina, with its horseshoe arch opening onto the souks.
bab jedid.c: A good entry point on foot into the medina from the south, towards the Zitouna.
bab jedid.d: The sixth gate cut through the medina’s ramparts in 1278, under the Hafsid sultan Abu Zakariya Yahya al-Wathiq. Nicknamed the ‘blacksmiths’ gate’ after the neighbouring souk. A rare medieval gate still in place, with its horseshoe arch.

bab menara.a: Nearby: Dar Othman, a sumptuous late 16th-century palace (Othman Dey), renowned for its façade.
bab menara.c: Simply a landmark marking the entrance to the Upper Medina; worth a quick visit.
bab menara.d: A neighbourhood on the south-western side of the medina, near Zitouna University, named after a former gate in the city walls that no longer exists.

bab saadoun.a: The monumental triple-arched gate, rebuilt in the 19th century, now stands alone on a roundabout to the north-west of the medina.
bab saadoun.c: Best viewed whilst passing by; as there is no interior to visit, plan for a quick stop.
bab saadoun.d: A monumental gate to the north-west of the Medina of Tunis, rebuilt in the 19th century with a triple arch.

bab souika.a: Nearby: the Youssef Saheb Ettabaa Mosque (1814), with its precious marble; the atmosphere of the singing cafés and evening events.
bab souika.c: L livelier in the evenings and during the festive season; a good starting point for a walk to Halfaouine.
bab souika.d: A square and working-class neighbourhood to the north of the medina, the heart of the city’s festive life: cafés with live music, the Sulâmiyya Sufi ensemble, Ramadan evenings (‘Layali Bab Souika’). The original gate, demolished in 1861, gave the place its name.

bahiret el bibane.a: Large south-eastern coastal lagoon, a Ramsar site important for fishing and birdlife.
bahiret el bibane.c: Binoculars are useful for birdwatching; light is best early in the morning.
bahiret el bibane.d: Large south-eastern coastal lagoon (Medenine), a Ramsar site since 2007, important for fishing and birdlife.

baptistere de sidi mansour.a: Ancient early Christian baptistery near Sidi Mansour, north of Sfax.
baptistere de sidi mansour.c: A secluded site: ask locally for directions.
baptistere de sidi mansour.d: Ancient baptistery near Sidi Mansour, north of Sfax.

bargou.a: A village nestled against the northern slope of Djebel Bargou, in a lush mountainous setting.
bargou.c: A starting point for hikes on Jebel Bargou; pleasant in spring.
bargou.d: A town nestled against the northern slope of Djebel Bargou (Siliana).

barrage barbara.a: The dam and its reservoir in Kroumirie, on the Oued el Kebir, set in wooded surroundings.
barrage barbara.c: Panoramic viewpoint along the forest roads of the north-west; lush green surroundings during the wet season.
barrage barbara.d: Dam and reservoir in Kroumirie, on the Oued el Kebir.

barrage de beni m'tir.a: A 1950s dam on the El Lil wadi, nestled in the cork oak forest of Kroumirie, south-west of Aïn Draham — one of Tunisia’s greenest landscapes.
barrage de beni m'tir.c: A lovely spot for a panoramic stop on the road to Ain Draham; a lush setting in spring, sometimes misty and cool in winter.
barrage de beni m'tir.d: Dam built between 1946 and 1953 on the Oued El Lil to the south-west of Ain Draham, in the wooded Kroumirie region. Irrigation, drinking water, hydroelectricity.

barrage de bou heurtma.a: The North-West Dam and its reservoir, in the Jendouba region.
barrage de bou heurtma.c: A nature stop on the region’s roads; best combined with visits to nearby ancient sites.
barrage de bou heurtma.d: North-western dam (Jendouba), with the raising of the dam completed in 2024, bringing the capacity to ~145 million m³.

barrage de joumine.a: The reservoir feeding Lake Ichkeul, in the south-west of the governorate of Bizerte.
barrage de joumine.c: A nature stop linked to the Ichkeul water system; worth seeing on the way to the park.
barrage de joumine.d: Reservoir feeding Lake Ichkeul, in the south-west of the governorate.

barrage de kasseb.a: The dam west of Béja, which supplies Greater Tunis with drinking water, at the foot of the Kroumirie.
barrage de kasseb.c: A leafy stop in spring; a stop-off on the forest roads of the Béja region.
barrage de kasseb.d: Dam to the west of Beja, supplying drinking water to Greater Tunis, at the foot of the Kroumirie.

barrage de sejnane.a: The dam and its reservoir on the Sejnane wadi, in the north-west of the governorate.
barrage de sejnane.c: Panoramic viewpoint on the road to Sejnane; worth combining with a visit to the neighbouring wetlands.
barrage de sejnane.d: Dam and reservoir on the Sejnane wadi, in the north-west of the governorate.

barrage de sidi el barrak.a: Large earth-fill dam near Tabarka, alongside a Ramsar-designated wetland: a reservoir ideal for observing waterbirds, in the wooded hinterland of Nefza.
barrage de sidi el barrak.c: Observe the birdlife around the reservoir; a nature stop-off on the road between Nefza and Tabarka. Check with local authorities before venturing off the tracks.
barrage de sidi el barrak.d: Earth-fill dam (~265 million m³) completed around 2000 (Beja), near Tabarka. Ramsar wetland.

barrage de sidi salem.a: The country’s largest dam on the Medjerda: a vast reservoir (~4,300 ha, ~555 million m³), offering sweeping views over the water and opportunities for freshwater fishing. Just a stone’s throw from Testour and its Andalusian medina.
barrage de sidi salem.c: Beautiful panoramic views from the surrounding area; well worth combining with a visit to Testour (mosque with an Andalusian minaret). An easy day trip from Béja or Medjez el-Bab.
barrage de sidi salem.d: Tunisia’s largest dam, completed in 1981 on the Medjerda near Testour (~555 million m³, reservoir area of 4,300 ha).

barrage de siliana.a: A dam on the Siliana wadi, set against a backdrop of plains and hills.
barrage de siliana.c: A simple scenic stop near Siliana.
barrage de siliana.d: A dam on the Siliana wadi, used for irrigation and water supply.

barrage lakhmess.a: A 32-metre gravity dam (1966) on the Lakhmess wadi, at the foot of Djebel Serj.
barrage lakhmess.c: Scenic stop-off point ~15 km south-east of Siliana, to be combined with a visit to Djebel Serj.
barrage lakhmess.d: A 32-metre gravity dam, inaugurated in 1966 on the Lakhmess wadi, approximately 15 km south-east of Siliana, at the foot of Djebel Serj.

barrage mellegue.a: A large 65-metre multi-arch dam (1949–1956) on the Mellegue wadi, set in a steep-sided wadi landscape.
barrage mellegue.c: Best visited in conjunction with the nearby village of Nebeur; pleasant views, no tourist facilities.
barrage mellegue.d: A 65-metre multi-arch dam on the Mellegue wadi, built between 1949 and 1956 (Le Kef). Irrigation, flood control, hydroelectricity.

basilique de chemtou.a: The Roman civil basilica in the heart of the ancient city of Simitthus.
basilique de chemtou.c: A stop on the Chemtou tour; best visited alongside the nearby theatre and Roman bridge.
basilique de chemtou.d: Roman civil basilica of Simitthus, in the heart of the ancient city.

basilique de damous el karita.a: The numerous column bases in the multiple naves of one of North Africa’s largest early Christian basilicas, and its underground rotunda.
basilique de damous el karita.c: A quiet part of Carthage; wear sturdy shoes for the grassy ground and the rotunda.
basilique de damous el karita.d: A vast early Christian basilica in Carthage, one of the largest in North Africa, with numerous naves and an underground rotunda.

basilique saint-pierre (dar el kous, le.a: One of the best-preserved early Christian buildings in Tunisia, with its apse and arches still intact.
basilique saint-pierre (dar el kous, le.c: A short visit to the heart of El Kef, to be included as part of a tour of the medina.
basilique saint-pierre (dar el kous, le.d: The ancient Christian basilica (known as Dar El Kous) in Le Kef, one of the best-preserved early Christian buildings in Tunisia.

bassins des aghlabides.a: The two large 9th-century circular stone basins that supplied Kairouan with water; the viewing platform overlooking them.
bassins des aghlabides.c: Climb up to the adjacent terrace to appreciate the geometry of the basins.
bassins des aghlabides.d: Open-air water reservoirs built around 860 to supply Kairouan, among the major hydraulic structures of the medieval Muslim world; a large circular basin approximately 128 m in diameter.

bataille de l'oued akarit.a: A memorial site for the battle of April 1943, in the area between the sea and the chotts north of Gabès.
bataille de l'oued akarit.c: A memorial site with no significant development: of mainly historical interest.
bataille de l'oued akarit.d: A battle during the Tunisian Campaign along the Akarit wadi, north of Gabès, in the area between the sea and the chotts.

bataille de thapsus (46 av. j.-c.).a: Presumed location of the battle where Caesar defeated the Pompeians and Juba I; there are no specific remains, only the coastal setting of Thapsus.
bataille de thapsus (46 av. j.-c.).c: More of a historical landmark than a site to visit; to be visited in conjunction with the ruins of Thapsus.
bataille de thapsus (46 av. j.-c.).d: Decisive battle in which Julius Caesar defeated the Pompeians led by Metellus Scipio and King Juba I, near Thapsus, bringing an end to the conflict in Africa. Presumed, approximate location.

bataille de zama (emplacement presume).a: No remains to be seen: this is a site commemorating Scipio’s victory over Hannibal (202 BC), the exact location of which remains a matter of debate.
bataille de zama (emplacement presume).c: A site of purely historical interest; the main attraction lies in the ancient cities in the surrounding area (Zama Regia, Naraggara).
bataille de zama (emplacement presume).d: Site of Scipio Africanus’s victory over Hannibal at the end of the Second Punic War. The exact location remains a matter of debate; presumed coordinates (Wikidata), to be regarded as approximate.

belkhir.a: Administrative centre of the Gafsa governorate.
belkhir.c: A place of passage: little major tourist interest.
belkhir.d: A town and the administrative centre of the Gafsa governorate.

ben gardane.a: A town in the south-east, a major cross-border commercial centre close to Libya.
ben gardane.c: Of mainly commercial and transit interest; check the latest news regarding the border area.
ben gardane.d: A town in the south-east near the Libyan border, an important cross-border trading centre.

beni khedache.a: A market town between Jebel Dahar and the Grand Erg, surrounded by ksour, a fortified granary and an underground mosque.
beni khedache.c: A good base for a tour of the ksours; make sure you stock up on water and fuel before heading off-road.
beni khedache.d: The town and administrative centre of Medenine (~30 km to the west), between Jebel Dahar and the Grand Erg Oriental. Ksour, a fortified granary and an underground mosque.

bisica lucana (henchir bichga).a: The scattered remains of the ancient Roman colony (thermal baths, traces of an aqueduct) in the countryside near Bou Arada; a modest site now in ruins.
bisica lucana (henchir bichga).c: Site poorly signposted, suitable for experienced visitors; best combined with a visit to nearby Avitta Bibba.
bisica lucana (henchir bichga).d: Roman city of Africa Proconsularis (Henchir Bichga, on the outskirts of Bou Arada, north of Siliana). Originally a colony, later a municipality: thermal baths, aqueduct, possible capitol, former bishop’s palace. Approximate coordinates (Pleiades).

blidet.a: An oasis village in the Nefzaoua region, within the Kebili oasis region.
blidet.c: A peaceful oasis stopover; the shade of the palm trees is a welcome relief in summer.
blidet.d: Oasis village in the governorate of Kebili, in the Nefzaoua oasis region.

bordj el hassar (kerkennah).a: A medieval fort with Spanish and Turkish influences on the Kerkennah archipelago, near El Abbassia.
bordj el hassar (kerkennah).c: Best combined with a tour of the archipelago and its traditional fishing practices.
bordj el hassar (kerkennah).d: Historic fort in the Kerkennah archipelago, near El Abbassia.

bordj lazarit (ghar el melh).a: The third of the 17th-century Ottoman forts at Ghar el Melh, near the ancient port of Porto Farina.
bordj lazarit (ghar el melh).c: Completes the tour of the three bordjs; allow half a day for the entire site and the lagoon.
bordj lazarit (ghar el melh).d: The Ottoman fort at Ghar el Melh, one of the three bordjs near the ancient port of Porto Farina.

borj el kebir (borj ghazi mustapha, djer.a: The largest coastal fort on Djerba, at Houmt Souk, rebuilt in the 16th century and associated with the corsair Dragut.
borj el kebir (borj ghazi mustapha, djer.c: Climb the ramparts for the view over the harbour; shade is scarce, so bring a hat.
borj el kebir (borj ghazi mustapha, djer.d: The coastal fort at Houmt Souk, the largest and best-preserved on Djerba, was rebuilt in the 16th century. Associated with the corsair Dragut.

borj el ksar (sfax).a: An 11th–12th-century corner fortification with three towers, housing a collection of stone carvings.
borj el ksar (sfax).c: Best combined with a walk along the medina’s ramparts.
borj el ksar (sfax).d: Fortification at the north-western corner of the Sfax medina (11th–12th centuries), featuring three towers. Houses a collection of stone carvings.

borj el woustani (ghar el melh).a: The central fort of Ghar el Melh, an Ottoman structure defending the former port of Porto Farina on the north coast.
borj el woustani (ghar el melh).c: A quick stop between the other two forts at Ghar el Melh; best combined with a visit to the nearby lagoon.
borj el woustani (ghar el melh).d: The middle fort of Ghar el Melh, an Ottoman structure defending the former port of Porto Farina on the north coast.

borj el-kebir de mahdia.a: The square fort overlooking the headland; the terraces opening out onto the sea and the nearby maritime cemetery.
borj el-kebir de mahdia.c: Visit at sunset for the view of Cape Africa.
borj el-kebir de mahdia.d: A fort at the tip of the Mahdia peninsula, built in the 16th century on older foundations. Panoramic views of Cape Africa and the old Fatimid harbour. Listed since 1912.

borj loutani (ghar el melh).a: One of the three 17th-century Ottoman forts built to protect the former pirate port of Porto Farina (Ghar el Melh).
borj loutani (ghar el melh).c: Well worth exploring as part of a tour of the three bordjs of Ghar el Melh; combine with a visit to the lagoon and its ramli gardens.
borj loutani (ghar el melh).d: One of the three Ottoman forts at Ghar el Melh (formerly Porto Farina), built in the 17th century to protect the corsair port.

bou arada.a: A town at the foot of Djebel Bargou, close to the ancient site of Apisa Maius.
bou arada.c: A stopover on the way to Djebel Bargou and the ruins of Apisa Maius.
bou arada.d: A town in the north of the Siliana governorate, at the foot of Djebel Bargou.

bouchemma.a: A locality in the Gabès Oasis (West Gabès).
bouchemma.c: A peaceful oasis stopover; little of major tourist interest.
bouchemma.d: A town and municipality in the Governorate of Gabès (West Gabès), within the Gabès Oasis.

boughrara.a: A coastal village on the mainland, near the ancient city of Gightis, facing Djerba.
boughrara.c: Best combined with a visit to the nearby ancient site of Gightis.
boughrara.d: A village on the mainland near the ancient city of Gightis, on the coast facing Djerba.

bulla regia.a: The villas with underground levels (House of the Hunt, House of Amphitrite) featuring mosaics in situ; the theatre and the baths of Julia Memmia.
bulla regia.c: Descend into the underground houses, which remain cool even in the height of summer; mosaics can be seen in situ.
bulla regia.d: A Roman town known for its villas with underground floors designed to provide relief from the heat, adorned with mosaics still in situ (House of the Hunt, House of Amphitrite).
bulla regia.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season; please check on site.

byrsa.a: The excavated Punic quarter on the hillside; the National Museum of Carthage; the panoramic view of the ancient harbours and the Gulf of Tunis.
byrsa.c: Head up in the late morning to catch the light over the bay, then carry on to the neighbouring Saint-Louis Cathedral.
byrsa.d: A hill that formed the acropolis of Punic Carthage, the site of the citadel, and later the monumental centre of Roman Carthage. Home to the National Museum of Carthage.
byrsa.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so check on site.

camp de concentration de kondas.a: Site of a former Second World War concentration camp; a place of remembrance with no significant remains.
camp de concentration de kondas.c: A site of remembrance rather than a tourist attraction; check locally for details.
camp de concentration de kondas.d: Former concentration camp in Kondas, Kairouan Governorate.

camp de concentration de meheri-zebbeus.a: Site of a camp established in 1939 in the Meknassy region; a place of remembrance.
camp de concentration de meheri-zebbeus.c: A memorial site with no tourist facilities; enquire locally.
camp de concentration de meheri-zebbeus.d: Former concentration camp established in 1939 in the Meknassy region.

camp de concentration de tniet-agareb.a: Site of a Second World War camp near Agareb; a place of remembrance.
camp de concentration de tniet-agareb.c: A memorial site with no tourist facilities; please enquire locally.
camp de concentration de tniet-agareb.d: Former Second World War concentration camp near Agareb.

cap angela (ras ben sakka).a: The headland is regarded as the northernmost point of the African continent, with its cliffs and wild coastline.
cap angela (ras ben sakka).c: Visit for the symbolic significance of Africa’s northernmost point and the panoramic views; the final stretch of track is rough, so ensure you have a suitable vehicle.
cap angela (ras ben sakka).d: A headland on the northern coast of Bizerte, considered the northernmost point of the African continent. Cliffs and wild coastline.

cap blanc (ras al-abiad).a: The white limestone promontory overlooking the sea, near Cape Angela, long presented as the northernmost point of Africa.
cap blanc (ras al-abiad).c: Combine with nearby Cape Angela; beautiful light and views of the coast at the end of the day.
cap blanc (ras al-abiad).d: A promontory of white limestone on the coast of Bizerte, long presented as the northernmost point of Africa, near Cape Angela.

cap bon.a: A peninsula with a rugged coastline between the Mediterranean and the Gulf of Tunis, alternating between rocky headlands, beaches and villages; renowned as a migration corridor for birds of prey at its northern tip.
cap bon.c: Ideal for a road trip (Korbous, El Haouaria, Kelibia); spring is the best time for observing migratory birds.
cap bon.d: A peninsula in north-eastern Tunisia with a rugged coastline between the Mediterranean Sea and the Gulf of Tunis. Coordinates at the northern tip of the cape.

cap carthage.a: The rocky headland on the coast north of Sidi Bou Said and La Marsa, with its views of the sea and the coastline.
cap carthage.c: Beautiful light at sunset; best combined with a stroll in Sidi Bou Said or La Marsa.
cap carthage.d: A rocky headland on the northern coast of Tunis, north of Sidi Bou Said and La Marsa.

cap gammarth.a: The cliffs and beaches of Gammarth north of La Marsa, and panoramic coastal views of the gulf.
cap gammarth.c: A lovely spot for a seaside stroll; picturesque sunsets over the coast.
cap gammarth.d: A headland on the coast north of La Marsa, with the cliffs and beaches of Gammarth.

cap negro (parc national jebel chitana-c.a: The cape and national park combine the Kroumirie coastal forest with sea cliffs in the north-west of the country.
cap negro (parc national jebel chitana-c.c: A wild and unspoilt site: make sure you have a suitable vehicle, plenty of water and are prepared for a walk to reach the viewpoints.
cap negro (parc national jebel chitana-c.d: The Kroumirie Cape and Coastal National Park, combining coastal forest and sea cliffs in the north-west of the country.

cap serrat.a: The headland and its sandy cove, situated between the forest and the lagoon and overlooked by a lighthouse, on the unspoilt Kroumirie coastline.
cap serrat.c: An ideal wild beach in summer; the access road is long, so bring provisions and water as there are few facilities.
cap serrat.d: A headland and sandy cove on the Kroumirie coast (Bizerte), nestled between woodland and a lagoon, dominated by a lighthouse. A preserved stretch of coastline.

cap sidi ali el mekki.a: The rocky headland enclosing Ghar el Melh Bay, with its popular beach and Ottoman fort, formerly known as Cape Farina.
cap sidi ali el mekki.c: A beautiful beach that gets very busy in summer: arrive early, and combine your visit with Raf Raf and the Ghar el Melh lagoon.
cap sidi ali el mekki.d: A rocky headland (formerly Cape Farina) enclosing Ghar el Melh Bay, a popular beach and an Ottoman fort.

cap zebib.a: The rocky headland on the north-eastern coast of Bizerte, extending into a series of small islets, in an area of cliffs and fishing grounds.
cap zebib.c: A peaceful coastal stop; best combined with the other headlands in the north of Bizerte.
cap zebib.d: A rocky headland on the north-eastern coast of Bizerte, extending into a series of small islets. An area of cliffs and fishing.

capitole de dougga.a: The tall façade with six Corinthian columns and its sculpted pediment; the podium overlooking the forum.
capitole de dougga.c: An iconic monument of the site; best photographed early in the day to avoid backlighting.
capitole de dougga.d: The Capitol of Thugga, dedicated to the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter, Juno, Minerva), was built in the 2nd century. Its colonnaded façade is one of the site’s most iconic monuments.
capitole de dougga.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary depending on the season, so please check on site.

capitole de sbeitla.a: The three distinct and well-preserved Capitoline temples, aligned behind the arch and the forum, represent a rare example of a triad comprising separate buildings.
capitole de sbeitla.c: Best combined with the wider Sufetula site in the immediate vicinity; just a few minutes are needed to see this highlight.
capitole de sbeitla.d: An exceptional complex of three distinct Capitoline temples dedicated to the triad, opening onto the Forum of Sufetula.
capitole de sbeitla.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary by season, so please check on site.

carrieres romaines de ghar el kebir (el.a: The vast underground chambers hewn from the sandstone from which the stones for Carthage were quarried; the skylights opening out onto the sea.
carrieres romaines de ghar el kebir (el.c: Best visited in conjunction with the tip of Cap Bon; the galleries offer a pleasant coolness in summer.
carrieres romaines de ghar el kebir (el.d: Vast underground quarries some 3 km west of El Haouaria, in operation from the Punic to the Roman periods; the sandstone was transported by sea to Carthage. Approximate coordinates.

carthage.a: Byrsa Hill and its museum; the circular and rectangular Punic harbours; the Antonine Baths by the sea; the Tophet of Salammbô and the Roman villas at the Odeon.
carthage.c: Allow half a day and buy the combined ticket valid for all areas, which are spread over several kilometres.
carthage.d: A city founded by the Phoenicians, capital of the Punic empire and later a major Roman city in Africa. An extensive archaeological site (the Byrsa hills, harbours, thermal baths) listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
carthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so check on site.

catacombes de sousse.a: A vast network of early Christian burial galleries dug beneath ancient Hadrumetum, containing thousands of tombs; only part of it is open to visitors.
catacombes de sousse.c: Check on arrival that the open section is accessible, as access to the catacombs is sometimes restricted.
catacombes de sousse.d: An extensive network of early Christian burial galleries dug beneath ancient Hadrumetum, containing thousands of tombs.
catacombes de sousse.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

cathedrale saint-louis de carthage.a: The Neo-Byzantine and Moorish façade; the interior, converted into a cultural centre (the Acropolium); the viewpoint on Byrsa Hill.
cathedrale saint-louis de carthage.c: Make the most of the terrace for the view, just after visiting the Carthage Museum.
cathedrale saint-louis de carthage.d: A former Catholic cathedral built in the late 19th century on Byrsa Hill. Now deconsecrated, it serves as a cultural centre (Acropolium).

cathedrale saint-vincent-de-paul de tuni.a: The Roman-Byzantine composite façade overlooking Habib Bourguiba Avenue, and the interior of the capital’s main Catholic church, which is still in use.
cathedrale saint-vincent-de-paul de tuni.c: Right in the heart of the modern city centre, well worth a visit at the start or end of a stroll along the avenue.
cathedrale saint-vincent-de-paul de tuni.d: Tunis Catholic Cathedral (late 19th century) on Habib Bourguiba Avenue, in a composite Roman-Byzantine style. Approximate coordinates.

centenarium tibubuci (ksar tarcine).a: Late Roman fort (c. 297–305) on the edge of the Grand Erg Oriental, part of the Limes; on the UNESCO Tentative List.
centenarium tibubuci (ksar tarcine).c: Access via a Saharan track: 4x4 vehicle and guide essential; ample water required.
centenarium tibubuci (ksar tarcine).d: Late Roman fort on the edge of the Grand Erg Oriental, part of the Limes Tripolitanus. UNESCO Tentative List.

chaouach (sua).a: The hilltop village of ancient Sua, dominated by a Byzantine fortress, with Roman and Christian ruins.
chaouach (sua).c: Mountain road north of Teboursouk: combine with a visit to neighbouring Toukabeur; wear sturdy footwear for the climb.
chaouach (sua).d: The hilltop village of ancient Sua, dominated by a Byzantine fortress, with Roman and Christian ruins. North of Teboursouk.

chemtou (simitthus).a: The Numidian yellow marble quarries; the Roman bridge over the Medjerda; the theatre, the basilica and the excellent marble museum.
chemtou (simitthus).c: Don’t miss the modern museum, which explains the quarrying of this famous ancient marble.
chemtou (simitthus).d: An ancient site famous for its quarries of Numidian yellow marble (marmor numidicum) exploited by the Romans, featuring a Roman bridge, theatre and basilica.
chemtou (simitthus).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so please check on site.

chenini (ksar et village).a: A hilltop Berber village centred around a ridge-top ksar and fortified granaries, with its white mosque below.
chenini (ksar et village).c: Ascent via a rocky path: wear sturdy footwear and visit early in the morning to avoid the heat.
chenini (ksar et village).d: A hilltop Berber village in the Tataouine region, organised around a ridge-top ksar and fortified granaries.

chenini nahal (gabes).a: A village and coastal oasis south-west of Gabès (date palms, henna); distinct from the Berber village of Chenini in Tataouine.
chenini nahal (gabes).c: A shaded stroll through the oasis; not to be confused with Chenini in Tataouine.
chenini nahal (gabes).d: A village and coastal oasis to the south-west of Gabès (date palms, henna). Distinct from the Berber village of Chenini in Tataouine.

chott el-fejaj.a: A long, salt-encrusted endorheic lake extending eastwards from Chott el-Jerid; it dries up for much of the year.
chott el-fejaj.c: Unmanaged salt flat: stay on the safe tracks and avoid the crust after rainfall.
chott el-fejaj.d: A long, muddy, endorheic lake arm extending eastwards from Chott el-Jerid, north of Nefzaoua. It dries up for much of the year.

chott el-gharsa.a: A salt depression, partly below sea level, north-west of Chott el-Jerid near Tozeur.
chott el-gharsa.c: The reflections and colours are at their most beautiful in low-angle light; stay on the trackable paths.
chott el-gharsa.d: A salt depression situated partly below sea level, north-west of Chott el-Jerid, near Tozeur.

chott el-jerid.a: The largest salt lake in the Tunisian Sahara, dry for much of the year, covered in salt crusts and mirages.
chott el-jerid.c: The road crosses the chott: stop at the designated viewing points at sunrise or sunset; the heat is stifling at midday.
chott el-jerid.d: The largest salt lake in the Tunisian Sahara, dry for much of the year and covered in salt crusts. Mirages and colourful reflections.

chott oulad amar.a: A salt flat (chott) in the Bekalta region, near Ras Dimass.
chott oulad amar.c: An undeveloped natural site; worth visiting, perhaps in conjunction with the nearby ruins of Thapsus.
chott oulad amar.d: A salt flat (chott) in the Bekalta region, near Ras Dimass.

chusira (kesra).a: The ancient remains of the Numidian city of Thusca, integrated into Kesra, Tunisia’s highest Berber village, with its terraced stone houses.
chusira (kesra).c: The hilltop village is just as worth visiting as the ruins; combine your visit with a trip to neighbouring Makthar and enjoy the panoramic views.
chusira (kesra).d: An ancient city beneath Kesra, the highest Berber village in Tunisia, near Makthar. The Numidian city of Thusca, a bishop’s seat.

cillium (kasserine).a: The theatre, the arch and, above all, the three-storey Mausoleum of the Flavii, in the ancient area on the outskirts of Kasserine.
cillium (kasserine).c: Approximate coordinates of the area: first locate the Mausoleum of the Flavii, which is the most visible feature.
cillium (kasserine).d: A Roman city near Kasserine, featuring a theatre, an arch and the Flavii mausoleum. Approximate coordinates of the ancient site.

cimetiere marin de mahdia.a: Historic cemetery facing the sea on the Mahdia peninsula; a peaceful setting by the coast.
cimetiere marin de mahdia.c: A place of contemplation: please visit with respect, especially at sunrise or sunset.
cimetiere marin de mahdia.d: Seaside cemetery on the Mahdia peninsula, overlooking the sea.

cimetiere militaire allemand de borj ced.a: The German military necropolis from the Second World War, with its massive crypt and graves clustered on the heights overlooking the gulf.
cimetiere militaire allemand de borj ced.c: An austere memorial site offering a view of the coast; a brief and sombre visit.
cimetiere militaire allemand de borj ced.d: German military necropolis for soldiers of the Second World War, with graves in Tunisia, on the heights of Borj Cedria.

cimetiere militaire de massicault (borj.a: The neat rows of headstones in the Commonwealth cemetery, set in well-maintained grounds, where soldiers from the 1943 Tunisian campaign are laid to rest.
cimetiere militaire de massicault (borj.c: A well-maintained place of remembrance; a sombre visit, best combined with a trip to the Medjerda Valley.
cimetiere militaire de massicault (borj.d: Commonwealth War Graves Cemetery (soldiers from the 1943 Tunisian campaign).

cimetiere militaire de ras rajel.a: The Commonwealth War Cemetery, where soldiers from the Tunisian campaign are laid to rest, in a well-maintained setting near Tabarka.
cimetiere militaire de ras rajel.c: A peaceful place of remembrance; a short stop on the road to Tabarka, to be visited with respect.
cimetiere militaire de ras rajel.d: Commonwealth War Graves Cemetery near Tabarka (soldiers from the Tunisian campaign).

citernes de bordj djedid (carthage).a: The extensive complex of vaulted Roman cisterns near the shore, distinct from those at La Malga, which contributed to Carthage’s water supply.
citernes de bordj djedid (carthage).c: An unassuming hydraulic monument to be included in the seaside tour of Carthage.
citernes de bordj djedid (carthage).d: A vast complex of Roman cisterns on the hill of Bordj Djedid in Carthage, near the shore, distinct from the cisterns at La Malga. Supplied by a vaulted aqueduct. Approximate coordinates.

citernes de la malga.a: The long series of parallel vaulted galleries of the immense Roman reservoir that received water from the Zaghouan aqueduct, parts of which have been reused for housing.
citernes de la malga.c: A quiet, off-the-beaten-track site; well worth a visit alongside the nearby Byrsa.
citernes de la malga.d: A complex of large Roman cisterns which stored the water supplied to Carthage by the Zaghouan aqueduct.

corbeille de nefta.a: A natural basket-shaped depression beneath the Nefta hills, fed by springs that irrigate the original oasis.
corbeille de nefta.c: The viewpoint offers the finest view; come at sunrise to catch the light.
corbeille de nefta.d: A natural basket-shaped depression beneath the Nefta hills, fed by springs that irrigate the original oasis. An iconic site in the Djerid.

cote corallienne de tabarka.a: The ‘Aiguilles’ rocks; the Genoese fort; the coral reefs, popular with divers.
cote corallienne de tabarka.c: A renowned diving spot; the jazz festival brings the town to life in summer.
cote corallienne de tabarka.d: The rocky coastline of Kroumirie, known for its ‘Aiguilles’ rock formations and coral reefs. Coordinates centred on the town.

dahmani (ebba ksour).a: A town (formerly Ebba Ksour) serving as a gateway to the nearby ancient site of Althiburos.
dahmani (ebba ksour).c: Make it your base for visiting nearby Althiburos.
dahmani (ebba ksour).d: A town in the Kef governorate, formerly known as Ebba Ksour, close to the ancient site of Althiburos.

dar ben abdallah.a: The columned courtyard with its fountain; the rooms recreating domestic life of yesteryear.
dar ben abdallah.c: The best place to gain an insight into the interior of a dar (patio house). Situated next to the Tourbet El Bey.
dar ben abdallah.d: An aristocratic palace dating from the late 18th century, now the Museum of Folk Arts and Traditions of Tunis. Surrounding a marble courtyard with a fountain, the richly decorated rooms — with painted wooden ceilings, chiselled stucco and faience — recreate the lifestyle of Tunis’s leading families: wedding scenes, costumes and ceremonial furniture.

dar el bey (palais du gouvernement).a: The imposing façade of the former Beylical palace in the Kasbah, now the seat of the Presidency of the Government, on Kasbah Square.
dar el bey (palais du gouvernement).c: An official building not open to the public: best viewed from the square, alongside the neighbouring Kasbah Mosque.
dar el bey (palais du gouvernement).d: Former Beylical palace in the Kasbah of Tunis, now the seat of the Presidency of the Government.

dar hussein.a: The marble porticoed courtyard, the painted ceilings, the sculpted stucco and the faience of this aristocratic palace, which houses the National Heritage Institute.
dar hussein.c: Access is sometimes restricted as it is an institutional site; well worth a visit whilst strolling through the lower medina.
dar hussein.d: An aristocratic palace in the medina of Tunis, with a porticoed courtyard, stucco and marble. Home to the National Heritage Institute.

dar lasram.a: The grand 18th-century patrician residence with its marble courtyard, ornate salons and driba (vestibule), headquarters of the Association for the Preservation of the Medina.
dar lasram.c: A fine example of Tunisian patrician architecture; well worth combining with a visit to the neighbouring palaces in the northern quarter of the medina.
dar lasram.d: A vast patrician residence in the medina of Tunis, built by the Lasram family. Headquarters of the Association for the Preservation of the Medina (ASM).

dar othman.a: The polychrome marble façade and ornate gateway of one of the oldest palaces in the medina, with its inner courtyard and garden.
dar othman.c: A little gem of residential architecture; a short visit to the heart of the medina.
dar othman.d: Othman Dey’s Palace in the medina of Tunis, with its polychrome marble façade, one of the city’s oldest palaces.

dar sghir (mahdia).a: A small museum housed in a traditional house in the medina, showcasing local architecture and arts.
dar sghir (mahdia).c: A quick stop during a stroll through the medina.
dar sghir (mahdia).d: Museum housed in a traditional house in the medina of Mahdia.

degache.a: An oasis town in the Jerid on the edge of the Chott el-Jerid, renowned for its deglet nour dates.
degache.c: A stop-off on the way to the chott; a stroll through the palm grove in the cooler hours of the day.
degache.d: An oasis town in the Jerid region north of Tozeur, on the edge of the Chott el-Jerid (deglet nour).

dehiba.a: A town in the east of Tataouine, a border crossing with Libya.
dehiba.c: Mainly of interest as a transit point; check the conditions in the border area.
dehiba.d: A town in the east of the Tataouine governorate, a border crossing with Libya.

djebel bargou.a: A mountain in the Dorsale range (1,266 m), source of the Miliane wadi, set in lush green surroundings.
djebel bargou.c: A lovely hiking area above Bargou; best visited in spring – do take water with you.
djebel bargou.d: A mountain in the north-central region (1,266 m) south-east of Siliana, forming the western axis of the Dorsale range. Source of the Wadi Miliane.

djebel bireno.a: Tunisia’s second-highest peak (1,419 m) and its Aleppo pine forest, from which zgougou is harvested.
djebel bireno.c: Mountain hike between Foussana and Thala; allow a full day, and bring water and sturdy footwear.
djebel bireno.d: Tunisia’s second-highest peak (1,419 m), between Foussana and Thala (Kasserine). A forest of Aleppo pines from which zgougou is harvested.

djebel boukornine.a: The distinctive twin peaks (‘the two horns’) overlooking Hammam Lif, its wooded paths and the view of the Gulf of Tunis.
djebel boukornine.c: Hike through the heart of the national park; set off from Hammam Lif – bring water and sturdy walking shoes.
djebel boukornine.d: A mountain with twin peaks (‘the two horns’) overlooking Hammam Lif and the Gulf of Tunis.

djebel bouramli.a: A mountain in the south-west extending from Djebel Orbata and bordering the Gafsa plain.
djebel bouramli.c: Arid terrain: suitable only for well-equipped walkers, with water supplies and an early start.
djebel bouramli.d: A mountain in the south-west (Gafsa), extending from Djebel Orbata and bordering the Gafsa plain.

djebel chambi (sommet).a: Tunisia’s highest peak (1,544 m) and its Aleppo pine forest, at the heart of a biosphere reserve.
djebel chambi (sommet).c: Climbing must be undertaken with a guide and a permit; check access conditions and set off early with plenty of water.
djebel chambi (sommet).d: Tunisia’s highest peak (1,544 m), on the Tunisian mountain range near Kasserine. A forested massif of Aleppo pines, at the heart of a biosphere reserve.

djebel chlel.a: Mountains in the east of the Sidi Bouzid governorate, near Ouled Haffouz.
djebel chlel.c: A largely unspoilt natural setting: make sure you bring water and sturdy footwear.
djebel chlel.d: Mountains in the east of the Sidi Bouzid governorate, near Ouled Haffouz.

djebel dahar.a: Arid plateau in the south-east, dotted with hilltop Berber villages and ksour, in the regions of Tataouine and Medenine.
djebel dahar.c: An ideal region for a tour of the ksour; a 4x4 or guide is useful for the tracks.
djebel dahar.d: Southeast mountain range (~713 m, ~6,500 km²), Tataouine and Medenine regions. An arid plateau dotted with hilltop Berber villages and ksour.

djebel dyr (dyr el kef).a: A table mountain (approx. 1,074 m) overlooking the town of Le Kef, built on its cliff face, offering sweeping panoramic views.
djebel dyr (dyr el kef).c: Climb up to the viewpoint overlooking El Kef and the plain, preferably in the late afternoon.
djebel dyr (dyr el kef).d: A table mountain in the Tunisian Atlas (approx. 1,074 m) overlooking the town of Le Kef, built on its cliff face.

djebel el haouaria.a: Terrain at the northern tip of Cap Bon, an important migration corridor for birds of prey.
djebel el haouaria.c: Spring is the best time of year to observe the passage of birds of prey; binoculars are essential.
djebel el haouaria.d: Terrain at the northern tip of Cap Bon, an important migration corridor for birds of prey. Approximate coordinates.

djebel ghorra.a: The highest peak in the Kroumirie (1,250 m), the wettest area in Tunisia and a nature reserve, on the Algerian-Tunisian border.
djebel ghorra.c: This hike is best undertaken in the warmer months; ensure you have suitable footwear, water and warm clothing, as the summit can be misty.
djebel ghorra.d: Highest peak in the Kroumirie (1,250 m), on the Algerian-Tunisian border, the wettest area in Tunisia. Nature reserve established in 2010.

djebel hammamet.a: Coastal mountain range to the south-west of Hammamet overlooking the bay.
djebel hammamet.c: A short hike offering scenic views; set off early to avoid the heat.
djebel hammamet.d: Coastal range to the south-west of Hammamet.

djebel ichkeul.a: The isolated limestone mountain overlooking the lake, with its Mediterranean flora and fauna and the hot springs at its foot.
djebel ichkeul.c: Hike up the park’s trails for views of the lake; binoculars are useful, and the best time to visit is from autumn to spring.
djebel ichkeul.d: An isolated limestone mountain overlooking Lake Ichkeul, within the national park. Mediterranean flora and fauna, with thermal springs at its foot.

djebel khroufa.a: The mountain and nature reserve in the Nefza region, a forested massif in the north-west.
djebel khroufa.c: A pleasant forest walk in spring and autumn; bring water and sturdy footwear.
djebel khroufa.d: Mountain and nature reserve in the Nefza region, a forested massif in the north-west.

djebel marchana.a: The wooded hills of southern Ben Arous, designated as a nature reserve, with its Mediterranean flora and fauna.
djebel marchana.c: A nature site with few facilities for walkers; check access details and bring water.
djebel marchana.d: The southern Ben Arous hills form a nature reserve, home to Mediterranean flora and fauna.

djebel mghila.a: The Dorsale Mountains (1,370 m) between Kasserine and Sidi Bouzid, at the heart of a national park established in 2010.
djebel mghila.c: Partly sensitive area: check access conditions before setting off on any hike.
djebel mghila.d: The Dorsale Mountain between Kasserine and Sidi Bouzid (1,370 m), at the heart of a national park established in 2010.

djebel orbata (sommet).a: A limestone mountain rising to 1,165 m east of Gafsa, protected by the national park.
djebel orbata (sommet).c: Climb reserved for walkers: set off early in the morning, take water and wear sturdy footwear.
djebel orbata (sommet).d: A limestone mountain (1,165 m) east of Gafsa, stretching some 60 km to the north-east. The landscape is protected by the national park. Approximate coordinates.

djebel ousselat.a: Limestone mountain in the Tunisian mountain range, the highest point in the Kairouan governorate, in the Oueslatia region.
djebel ousselat.c: Mid-mountain hike: make sure you wear suitable footwear and take plenty of water.
djebel ousselat.d: Limestone mountain in the Tunisian mountain range, the highest point in the governorate of Kairouan (Oueslatia).

djebel ressas.a: The iconic limestone silhouette to the south-east of Tunis, with its cliffs, old lead mine tunnels and panoramic views from the heights.
djebel ressas.c: A hike for experienced walkers; set off early, take water and wear sturdy footwear; views over Greater Tunis from the summit.
djebel ressas.d: An isolated limestone massif (~795 m) south-east of Tunis, a landmark of Greater Tunis. Former lead mines (the name means ‘lead mountain’). Approximate coordinates.

djebel semmama.a: A wooded mountain in the Dorsale range (1,314 m), aligned with Djebel Chambi.
djebel semmama.c: Check access conditions before setting out on any hike in this area.
djebel semmama.d: A mountain in the Dorsale range in the governorate of Kasserine (1,314 m), aligned with Djebel Chambi.

djebel serj.a: A limestone mountain (1,357 m) featuring the Ain Dhab Cave and forests of Aleppo pine and holm oak.
djebel serj.c: Approx. 20 km south-east of Siliana; a pleasant nature walk in spring – bring water and walking shoes.
djebel serj.d: A limestone mountain, 1,357 m high, approximately 20 km south-east of Siliana. Ain Dhab Cave, forests of Aleppo pine and holm oak.

djebel tebaga.a: Mountain range north of Chott el-Jerid with Permian fossil reefs; site of the Tebaga breakthrough (1943).
djebel tebaga.c: Of geological and historical interest; arid terrain – bring water and a hat.
djebel tebaga.d: Mountain range north of Chott el-Jerid near Kebili, featuring fossilised reefs from the Permian marine period. Site of the Tebaga breakthrough (Battle of the Mareth Line, 1943).

djebel trozza.a: Mountain range in the Kairouan governorate, near Haffouz.
djebel trozza.c: Rural, largely undeveloped landscape: make sure you bring water and wear suitable footwear.
djebel trozza.d: Mountain range in the Kairouan governorate, near Haffouz.

djebel zaghouan.a: The limestone summit overlooking the plain (1,295 m) and its sweeping panoramic views of north-eastern Tunisia from the ridges.
djebel zaghouan.c: A climb for experienced walkers; set off early, take water and a windbreaker; clear views on a clear day.
djebel zaghouan.d: A limestone peak rising to 1,295 m, one of the highest in north-eastern Tunisia. It overlooks the Zaghouan plain.

dougga (thugga).a: the Capitol with its Corinthian columns; the theatre set against the hillside; the Libyco-Punic mausoleum; the Place des Vents and the latrines with twelve seats.
dougga (thugga).c: Extensive ruins on a slope: walking shoes and at least two hours; magnificent in the low morning sun.
dougga (thugga).d: An ancient city of Numidian and later Roman origin, it is one of the best-preserved ancient sites in North Africa (capitol, theatre, temples, Libyco-Punic mausoleum). Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
dougga (thugga).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; opening hours vary according to the season, so check on site.

douiret (ksar et village).a: A Berber cave village and its hilltop ksar, long inhabited by an Amazigh community.
douiret (ksar et village).c: Steep, exposed terrain: bring water, a hat and walking shoes.
douiret (ksar et village).d: A Berber cave village and its hilltop ksar, south-west of Tataouine, long inhabited by an Amazigh community.

dunes de douz.a: The gateway to the Sahara: the vast dunes of the Grand Erg Oriental, accessible from Douz.
dunes de douz.c: Camel treks or 4x4 trips at sunrise/sunset for the most beautiful light; extreme heat during the day.
dunes de douz.d: Nicknamed the ‘Gateway to the Sahara’, Douz provides access to the great dunes of the Grand Erg Oriental. Coordinates centred on the town.

ecomusee de l'ichkeul.a: Exhibits on the flora, fauna and geology of Ichkeul National Park, at the foot of Djebel Ichkeul.
ecomusee de l'ichkeul.c: The ideal starting point for a visit to the park; start here to get an understanding of the site before climbing Djebel Ichkeul.
ecomusee de l'ichkeul.d: Ichkeul National Park Ecomuseum (fauna, flora, geology), at the foot of Djebel Ichkeul.
ecomusee de l'ichkeul.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening times on site.

edifice a colonnes de carthage.a: The Roman colonnaded monument in the archaeological site, near the villas on the Odeon Hill.
edifice a colonnes de carthage.c: A modest ruin to include in a walk around the Roman villas.
edifice a colonnes de carthage.d: Roman colonnaded monument in the archaeological area of Carthage, near the Roman villas.

eglise de l'immaculee-conception de kair.a: Catholic church inherited from the French Protectorate, a testament to the city’s colonial heritage.
eglise de l'immaculee-conception de kair.c: Check opening times on arrival, as the building is not always open.
eglise de l'immaculee-conception de kair.d: Catholic church in Kairouan, a legacy of the French Protectorate.

eglise notre-dame-du-mont-carmel de mahd.a: A Catholic church from the colonial era, bearing witness to Mahdia’s diverse past.
eglise notre-dame-du-mont-carmel de mahd.c: Opening hours vary: please check on site.
eglise notre-dame-du-mont-carmel de mahd.d: The Catholic church in Mahdia, dating from the colonial era.

eglise notre-dame-du-rosaire de beja.a: The Catholic church, built during the Protectorate era, bears witness to Béja’s colonial heritage.
eglise notre-dame-du-rosaire de beja.c: A brief stop in the town centre, well worth including in your tour of Béja.
eglise notre-dame-du-rosaire de beja.d: Catholic church built during the Protectorate era in Beja.

eglise saint-alexandre-nevski de bizerte.a: The Russian Orthodox church dating from 1939, built by sailors from the Russian fleet who took refuge in Bizerte after 1920.
eglise saint-alexandre-nevski de bizerte.c: A small, distinctive building in the town; a brief visit, best combined with a tour of Bizerte’s town centre.
eglise saint-alexandre-nevski de bizerte.d: Russian Orthodox Church in Bizerte, built by sailors from the Russian fleet who took refuge there after 1920.

eglise saint-joseph de tunis.a: The Catholic church dating from the Protectorate era and its interior, in the modern part of Tunis.
eglise saint-joseph de tunis.c: Well worth a look whilst strolling through the colonial city centre.
eglise saint-joseph de tunis.d: A Catholic church in the modern part of Tunis, built during the Protectorate era.

eglise saint-pierre-et-saint-paul de sfa.a: A Catholic church dating from the colonial era, reflecting Sfax’s diverse heritage.
eglise saint-pierre-et-saint-paul de sfa.c: Opening times vary: please check on site.

eglise sainte-helene de zaghouan.a: The former Catholic church from the Protectorate period in the town of Zaghouan, a fine example of colonial architecture.
eglise sainte-helene de zaghouan.c: A small heritage site worth seeing whilst passing through Zaghouan.
eglise sainte-helene de zaghouan.d: Former Catholic church in the town of Zaghouan, a reminder of the Protectorate period.

eglise sainte-jeanne-d'arc de tunis.a: The colonial-era architecture of this church in the northern district (Lafayette) of modern Tunis.
eglise sainte-jeanne-d'arc de tunis.c: Of architectural interest above all; a brief stop in the modern city centre.
eglise sainte-jeanne-d'arc de tunis.d: Catholic church in the northern district of Tunis (Lafayette), featuring colonial-era architecture.

eglise sainte-maxime de tabarka.a: The former church, converted in the late 19th century from a Roman cistern, now a museum, in the centre of Tabarka.
eglise sainte-maxime de tabarka.c: A short visit to include as part of a stroll through the town; best combined with a visit to the nearby Genoese fort.
eglise sainte-maxime de tabarka.d: A former church converted between 1884 and 1891 from a Roman cistern. Now deconsecrated, it houses a museum; listed in 2016.

el abbassia (kerkennah).a: A village in the Kerkennah Archipelago, near Bordj El Hassar Fort.
el abbassia (kerkennah).c: A convenient starting point for visiting the nearby fort.
el abbassia (kerkennah).d: A village in the Kerkennah Archipelago, near Bordj El Hassar Fort.

el alia.a: The Andalusian town renowned for its chechia craftsmanship and textile traditions.
el alia.c: Discover the chechia workshops; a short visit, best combined with a tour of the region’s other Andalusian towns.
el alia.d: A town of Andalusian origin renowned for its chechia craftsmanship and textile traditions.

el aouja (site de ceramique sigillee).a: An ancient site known as the place where sigillata pottery was discovered; the surface remains are not particularly spectacular.
el aouja (site de ceramique sigillee).d: An ancient archaeological site known as the site where sigillata pottery was discovered.

el ayoun.a: A town in the north of the Kasserine governorate, with no notable monuments.
el ayoun.d: A town and sub-prefecture in the north of the Kasserine governorate.

el faouar.a: A Saharan oasis town and the administrative centre of the Kebili governorate.
el faouar.c: Starting point for trips into the desert; extreme heat in summer, so set off early.
el faouar.d: Town and administrative centre of the Kebili governorate, a Saharan oasis settlement.

el guettar.a: An oasis town famous for the El Guettar Hermaion (Mousterian/Aterian) and the battle of 1943.
el guettar.c: The prehistoric context is best understood through the nearby Gafsa Museum.
el guettar.d: An oasis town south-east of Gafsa, famous for the El Guettar Hermaion (Mousterian/Aterian) and the Battle of El Guettar (1943).

el hamma (gabes).a: A thermal oasis town renowned since ancient times for its hot springs which feed the hammams.
el hamma (gabes).c: The springs are very hot: check which pools are open to visitors.
el hamma (gabes).d: A thermal oasis town some 30 km west of Gabès, renowned since ancient times for its hot springs which supply its hammams.

el hamma du jerid.a: Oasis town on the northern edge of the Djerid, irrigated by hot springs.
el hamma du jerid.c: Very hot springs: enquire about the pools accessible to visitors.
el hamma du jerid.d: Oasis town in the governorate of Tozeur, on the northern edge of the Djerid, with hot springs. Palm grove irrigated by thermal springs.

el kantara (djerba).a: A town situated on the site of the Roman road linking the island to the mainland towards Zarzis.
el kantara (djerba).c: A crossing point on the road: convenient for reaching the mainland.
el kantara (djerba).d: A town in south-eastern Djerba, situated on the site of the Roman road linking the island to the mainland towards Zarzis.

el krib.a: A modern town adjacent to the ancient site of Musti, with its Arch of Gordian III and its macellum.
el krib.c: Park at El Krib to visit Musti on foot, which is right next door.
el krib.d: A town in the north of the Siliana governorate, close to the ancient site of Musti.

el ksour (le kef).a: A small town and municipality in the Kef Governorate, with no major monuments.
el ksour (le kef).c: A simple stopover in the region.
el ksour (le kef).d: A town and municipality in the Kef Governorate.

el metouia.a: An oasis town north of Gabès, in the Gulf Oasis.
el metouia.c: A cool stroll under the palm trees is possible during the hottest part of the day.
el metouia.d: An oasis settlement and sub-prefecture of the Gabès Governorate, to the north of the city.

embouchure de la medjerda.a: The delta of Tunisia’s main river, its alluvial plain and the coastal wetland rich in birdlife, near Kalaat el-Andalous.
embouchure de la medjerda.c: Combine this with a visit to the hilltop village of Kalaat el-Andalous; an excellent spot for birdwatching.
embouchure de la medjerda.d: The delta and mouth of the Medjerda, Tunisia’s main river, on the north coast near Kalaat el-Andalous. Alluvial plain and coastal wetland.

enfida (enfidaville).a: A town in the Sahel region near ancient Uppenna; a museum of early Christian mosaics and a Commonwealth war cemetery from the 1942–1943 campaign.
enfida (enfidaville).c: The Enfida Museum and the military cemetery are the two main points of interest.
enfida (enfidaville).d: A town in the Sahel near the ancient site of Uppenna. Museum of early Christian mosaics; Commonwealth war cemetery (1942–1943).

erriadh (hara seghira, djerba).a: A former neighbourhood with a strong Jewish community, home to the Ghriba Synagogue and the Djerbahood street murals (2014).
erriadh (hara seghira, djerba).c: Wander through the narrow streets on foot to discover the murals; go early in the morning for the best light.
erriadh (hara seghira, djerba).d: A village south of Houmt Souk, a former neighbourhood with a strong Jewish community (Hara Sghira). Home to the Ghriba Synagogue and the Djerbahood murals (2014).

fatnassa.a: Oasis village on the southern shore of Chott el-Jerid, in the Souk Lahad district.
fatnassa.c: A peaceful oasis stop; the shade of the palm trees is welcome in summer.
fatnassa.d: Oasis village in the Souk Lahad district, on the southern shore of Chott el-Jerid.

feriana.a: A town near the extensive ancient site of Thelepte.
feriana.c: Make this your starting point for visiting Thelepte, some 5 km away.
feriana.d: A town in the south-west of the governorate of Kasserine, close to the ancient site of Thelepte.

ferme des lars / dome (chott el-djerid,.a: Exterior set of the Lars’ farm (the dome) built on the Chott el-Djerid, west of Nefta, for Star Wars.
ferme des lars / dome (chott el-djerid,.c: Access via the track across the chott: a 4x4 is recommended, and do come early in the morning to enjoy the light and the cool air.
ferme des lars / dome (chott el-djerid,.d: The exterior set of the Lars’ farm (the dome/igloo), built on the Chott el-Djerid to the west of Nefta for Star Wars IV (1977), and rebuilt for Episodes II and III. Distinct from Tozeur and Nefta.

foret de dar chichou.a: A state-owned dune forest covering more than 6,000 ha north of El Haouaria, resulting from the stabilisation of the Cap Bon dunes which began around 1930.
foret de dar chichou.c: A pleasant setting for a nature break between the capes; please stay on the tracks.
foret de dar chichou.d: Cap Bon State Forest (>6,000 ha) north of El Haouaria (Nabeul). A Mediterranean dune forest resulting from dune stabilisation work begun around 1930.

fort d'espagne (bizerte).a: The 16th-century fort perched on the heights of Bizerte, overlooking the town and the harbour, a testament to the Spanish-Ottoman rivalry.
fort d'espagne (bizerte).c: Head up at the end of the day for panoramic views of the town and the sea; accessible by car or a short walk.
fort d'espagne (bizerte).d: A fort on the heights of Bizerte (16th century), dating from the period of Spanish-Ottoman rivalry in the Mediterranean. It overlooks the town and the harbour.

fort de kelibia (borj el-kebir).a: The fortress overlooking the harbour and the beach; the remodelled Byzantine ramparts; the view across the Cap Bon coast, stretching as far as Sicily on a clear day.
fort de kelibia (borj el-kebir).c: An easy climb from the harbour; superb panoramic views at sunset.
fort de kelibia (borj el-kebir).d: A citadel on a 150-metre promontory overlooking the sea and Kelibia, north-east of Cape Bon. It features Roman and Byzantine elements, but the bulk of the structure dates from a 16th-century reconstruction with Ottoman additions.

fort de la goulette (karraka).a: The 16th-century Ottoman and Spanish fortress guarding the entrance to Lake Tunis; the massive bastions.
fort de la goulette (karraka).c: Worth seeing whilst passing through La Goulette, renowned for its fish restaurants.
fort de la goulette (karraka).d: The coastal fortress of La Goulette (La Karraka), commanding the entrance to the port of Tunis, built in the 16th century and contested between the Spanish and the Ottomans.

fort genois de tabarka.a: The Genoese fort perched on its islet connected to the coast; the ramparts and the panoramic view over the bay and the Aiguilles.
fort genois de tabarka.c: Head up there in the late afternoon for the view of the famous Aiguilles rocks.
